items.title: Rotate a leaked GitLab token and let GitLab Duo fix the code
items.summary: Secret detection alerts you when an active personal access token (PAT) is exposed in your default branch. Acting on that finding is harder: revoking the token breaks dependent pipelines, and replacing it safely takes several manual steps. While the finding waits in your vulnerability report, the token stays live.Starting in GitLab 19.6 in beta for GitLab Ultimate, you can remediate a leaked GitLab PAT directly from the vulnerability page. Select Rotate and fix, and GitLab revokes the token, stores a replacement in GitLab Secrets Manager, and uses GitLab Duo Agent Platform to open a merge request (MR) to update your CI/CD jobs. You review and merge the MR. GitLab never exposes the new token value to you or your agents.Why leaked tokens stay active after detectionImagine that secret detection flags an active PAT in deploy.sh:export GITLAB_TOKEN="glpat-..."Fixing this manually requires tracking down the token's owner, revoking it, generating a replacement with matching scopes, storing it securely, and opening MRs to update your scripts and CI/CD jobs.Because this process is tedious, remediations often stall or go wrong:The finding ages: Nobody wants to break the pipeline, so the finding sits in the vulnerability report while the token remains active.The fix stops halfway: Someone revokes the token immediately, breaking the build. In a rush to recover, they paste a replacement into a less secure CI/CD variable.The new token leaks: Someone shares the replacement token in a chat thread so a teammate can configure it.In the gap between detected and rotated, the token still works for anyone who can read the repository.Rotate and fix in a snapThe Rotate and fix function closes this gap by combining secret detection and validity checks, GitLab Secrets Manager, and GitLab Duo Agent Platform.When you open an active PAT finding and select AI actions > Fix with AI > Rotate and fix, GitLab:Revokes the leaked token and creates a replacement with the same name, scopes, and duration (reset from the rotation date).Stores the new value as a project secret in Secrets Manager, available to all branches and environments.Marks the token as inactive on the vulnerability.Starts a GitLab Duo Developer Flow session, which opens an MR to remove the hardcoded token and configure your CI/CD jobs to read the secret.You review the MR, merge it, and resolve the vulnerability.Update the code without exposing the new tokenRotation finishes before the agent starts, so GitLab Duo never sees the new token. By the time GitLab Duo reads the file to remove the hardcoded credential, the value is revoked and the replacement is safely stored in Secrets Manager. The agent receives only the vulnerability and its file location, the new secret's name, and your username so it can assign the MR to you. GitLab Duo then updates your pipeline configuration:deploy:  secrets:    GITLAB_TOKEN:      gitlab_secrets_manager:        name: ROTATED_GITLAB_TOKEN_123      file: false  script:    - ./deploy.shYour script continues using GITLAB_TOKEN, which Secrets Manager injects at runtime.What to know before you implementAvailability: This beta feature requires GitLab Ultimate 19.6 or later. It is enabled by default on GitLab.com, available behind the secrets_manager_pat_rotation feature flag on GitLab Self-Managed, and not yet available on GitLab Dedicated.Supported secret types: Rotation supports GitLab PATs, including fine-grained PATs. It doesn't yet cover other secrets that secret detection finds, such as cloud provider keys.Immediate and irreversible: The leaked token stops working right away, and you can't undo the rotation. Scripts outside GitLab CI/CD and jobs in other projects that used the old token need a new token, because the new secret is scoped only to the current project and its raw value cannot be retrieved.Ownership rules: On GitLab.com, you can rotate only your own tokens. On GitLab Self-Managed, administrators can also rotate tokens belonging to other users.Independent of AI: If the GitLab Duo session cannot start, GitLab still rotates the old token and stores the replacement so you can update the code manually.For role requirements, required settings, and step-by-step instructions, see the leaked token rotation documentation.Automate rotation across a groupRotating tokens one by one doesn't scale across large organizations. Rotate and fix makes two API calls: the projectSecretCreateFromLeakedToken GraphQL mutation, which rotates the token and stores the secret, and a request that starts the GitLab Duo Developer Flow.   We packaged both calls into leaked-token-rotation-automation, a dependency-free Python CLI and CI/CD component that batch-rotates tokens across an entire group:Active vulnerability findings: Rotates active leaked PATs across your group's repositories and opens an MR for each finding. On GitLab.com, it rotates your own tokens and lists other users' tokens in the report for follow-up. On GitLab Self-Managed, an administrator can rotate

items.title: Turn Slack conversations into trusted software, faster
items.summary: Most software starts as a conversation: a customer requests a new capability, a product manager weighs it against the roadmap, an engineer checks feasibility, and a security lead asks what it touches.Then someone has to turn it into work. They reread the thread, retype the decisions into an issue, and hope they didn’t miss an important detail buried in a reply. The conversation moves fast; the handoff between both teams and tools is where it slows.AI agents are uniquely equipped for that handoff: reading a long, many-voiced discussion and turning it into structured work. That leaves people free to collaborate while agents produce the output.GitLab for Slack now adds agentic capabilities and is in limited availability for GitLab.com users with GitLab 19.6. Access for GitLab Self-Managed and GitLab Dedicated will follow in GitLab 19.7, when GitLab for Slack becomes generally available. Mention @GitLab in a thread in your team's channels, and the agent reads the conversation, finds what already exists, turns decisions into tracked work, and starts the agent flows that carry it to production. Work starts in Slack and lands in GitLab, where it's governed, tracked, and delivered."Teams make decisions in Slack every day, and the best agents are the ones that can act on that context. GitLab for Slack lets agents read the conversation, take action across the software lifecycle in GitLab, and bring the results back to the thread. Teams can go from a quick discussion to planned, reviewed, and shipped work without switching tools."– Katie Steigman, Vice President Product Management, SlackSlack is the front door, GitLab does the workGitLab for Slack connects the interface where your team discusses the work to the platform where your software ships. Your team’s conversation in Slack itself becomes the agent's input, so no decision gets lost between the thread and the first commit.The agent also looks beyond the thread. When you mention @GitLab, it can read the messages in the channel where you mentioned it, so its response reflects the whole discussion and not only the replies under one message. You can also ask it to catch you up first, for example: “@GitLab, summarize #channel for me.”It works in both directions. GitLab context (what's been built, what's tracked, whether a merge request is ready, etc.) also shows up in the conversation. The conversation becomes issues, merge requests, and running agent flows, with results posted back to the thread.If your team already uses the GitLab for Slack app on GitLab.com, reinstall it today to add these agent capabilities. There's nothing new to learn; you just mention @GitLab.Use it where your team worksDebate it in the channel. Draft it in your DM. GitLab for Slack works in both places:Public and private channels: Bring the agent into team discussions and turn decisions into tracked work where everyone can see it.Your own DM: Get a private space to ask questions, check on a merge request, or draft an issue before you share anything with the team.One thread, every roleGitLab for Slack works for everyone who shapes the work, including people who never write code:Product managers turn a decision into scoped work before the meeting ends.Designers send their notes straight to the people and agents doing the work.Sales and customer teams bring a customer request into a team channel and follow it to production.Security and platform teams confirm agent work passes review before it ships.Engineers check what exists before building it again, without leaving the conversation.Watch GitLab for Slack in action:   Governed from the first mentionAn agent that acts from a chat thread is only useful if you can trust what it does. The conversation happens in Slack; the work and every control stay in GitLab.Agents act only when asked. In channels, GitLab acts only when someone mentions @GitLab. In your own DM, it answers you and only you.Internal conversations only. GitLab for Slack doesn't run in external (Slack Connect) channels, so project context isn't exposed to people outside your organization.Requests run as you. Each request uses the requester's linked GitLab account, scoped to their existing permissions. If you don't have access to a project in GitLab, the agent can't access it for you in Slack.Context stays in scope. The agent reads the surrounding context only from the channel where it was mentioned. Anything it does in GitLab still follows your permissions.Actions are on the record. Each request creates an agent session in GitLab. Merge requests go through the same reviews, approval rules, and audit trail as any other change.Costs stay visible. Usage draws from your GitLab Credits, so admins can track and cap it like any other agent work.This is the model behind GitLab's governed software factory: agents speed up the work, and source control, security, and governance keep it trustworthy. Slack is one more way into that factory, not a way around it.Get startedGitLab for Slack is in lim

items.title: Keep recurring work moving with scheduled automations
items.summary: Every engineering team has work that needs regular attention, like triaging new issues or investigating incidents. Among DevSecOps professionals using AI tools, 43% say automating repetitive tasks has created the most efficiency, according to GitLab’s Global DevSecOps report. But agents still rely on a human to kick off the workflow or an event trigger to fire, and without a record of what ran and why, no one can trace how the work got done.With scheduled automations, in beta in GitLab 19.6, flows in GitLab Duo Agent Platform handle routine tasks on a schedule your team sets and keep a history of what ran. Scheduled automations are a building block of the governed software factory, where agents and flows work autonomously within controls set by your team.Put routine work on a scheduleRelying on a person or an event to start automated work limits efficiency gains and makes timing unpredictable. When the person responsible is out, the work waits, and when there’s no event, it never starts. Scheduled automations give routine work a dependable rhythm.You can already run event-based automations in GitLab Duo Agent Platform, triggered by activities like a merge request or a mention in a comment. Scheduled automations start the work on a recurring schedule, with no event needed. Describe the task in plain language, set the cadence once, and the automation runs on its own at the times you choose, with run counts and success rates your team can review.Triage new issues daily to keep your backlog organized, or schedule a flow to check CI health incidents every hour and comment with the likely root cause, so the investigation is underway before anyone opens the issue.You can set a schedule from every 15 minutes to every month, at the time of day and in the timezone that meets the needs of your group. Because automations in GitLab drive the work your whole team depends on, each one runs at the project level.See how to schedule an automation, from describing the task to reviewing its first run:   Control and transparency for every runAs agents take on more of the work around your code, teams need to know which agent acted, what permissions it had, and what it did. Without a verifiable identity and a record of every change, no one can say which agent made a change or why it ran, and every review or audit starts with reconstruction. It’s hard to scale agentic work when you can’t see what agents or flows already did.Scheduled automations offer the controls a team needs to trust what runs on its own. Each automation runs as a dedicated service account with scoped permissions, so your team can tell agent work from human work in the audit events. Audit events also record changes to every automation, so your team knows what ran, what happened, and who changed it.A redesigned Automations page, previously labeled Triggers, brings scheduled and event-based automations together in one place, with run volume, success rate, and session details for each, so your team can see details of what ran and what happened. If a run fails, the page shows the reason, and you can open the session to see exactly what the agent did.A foundation of the governed software factoryThe governed software factory is a connected system for moving software from idea to production under your organization’s own policy and standards, with an evidence chain that records how every change got there.Scheduled automations add a critical piece to that foundation by automating work into the factory on a regular basis. A weekly scan for vulnerabilities can create work items for the factory to act on, and every automation runs as its own service account with scoped permissions, so its actions stay easy to identify.Scheduling the right work keeps the factory moving, saves your team time, and leaves a record they can trust. Creating one of these automations is a good place to start:CI health investigation - An hourly check of open incidents that comments with the likely root cause, so the investigation is underway before anyone opens the issue.Issue triage - A morning review of new issues that decides whether each is a bug or a feature and adds a label, so the backlog stays organized.Stale work report - A weekly report that lists the open issues with no activity in the last 30 days in a new issue, so stuck work gets a second look.Duplicate spotting - A daily check of new issues that comments with any open issues that look like the same request, so duplicates get linked before anyone triages them twice.Weekly digest - A Friday summary of what closed and merged that week, written in plain language for people outside engineering and posted as a new issue, so stakeholders know what shipped without reading MR titles.Try scheduled automations todayScheduled automations are available now in beta in GitLab 19.6. items.title: Cut your vulnerability backlog with agentic remediation
items.summary: Vulnerability backlogs are growing faster than teams can clear them. AI writes more code and finds more flaws, while fixes still move at human speed. NIST’s National Vulnerability Database has already published twice as many CVEs in 2026 as in all of 2025, and ceased enriching most CVEs this past April.Compounding the problem, a finding that looks safe to defer may not stay that way. Attackers now use AI to find and exploit flaws in hours, even those long written off as theoretical. In October, frontier models uncovered PHP2Shell, a pair of unauthenticated remote code execution bugs in PHP that had been dismissed as unexploitable in 2012.Discovery and exploitation now run at machine speed. To keep up, defenders need agentic security tools that detect and remediate vulnerabilities with minimal manual effort while leaving teams in full control.GitLab 19.6 helps teams shrink their security findings backlog. Security managers can now turn on agentic triage and remediation across entire groups of projects without scripting against the API. A new agentic flow adds exploitability context to static application security testing (SAST) findings, so teams can prioritize the ones that pose real risk. Security leaders can then track the results on a new mean time to remediation (MTTR) chart.Find and fix faster with agentic securityGitLab 19.6 builds on a platform that finds and fixes vulnerabilities with agentic security. GitLab Duo security agents use frontier AI reasoning to examine your codebase and every merge request for the logic flaws scanners miss, while built-in scanners catch known vulnerabilities from source to runtime. Agents filter out false positives before they reach a developer's queue, then help teams prioritize the rest by severity, exploitability, reachability, and blast radius. GitLab Orbit, our native knowledge graph, grounds that reasoning in the live state of your system.For confirmed findings, an agent writes a fix, opens a merge request, and triggers the pipeline to rerun tests and scans. If anything fails, the agent reads the logs, revises the fix, and retests. Developers review a ready-to-merge fix with the agent's rationale and confidence score. That fix goes through the same approvals as any other change, and neither developers nor agents can bypass them. Remediation keeps pace with discovery, and the backlog shrinks.GitLab 19.6 advances agentic remediationGitLab 19.6 puts agents to work across more of that backlog. It extends agentic triage and remediation to more projects, adds exploitability context to SAST findings, and charts MTTR.Turn on agents across many projectsAgents shrink the backlog only where they run, and turning them on one project at a time doesn't scale to thousands. Automated triage and remediation (ATR) profiles let security managers turn on agentic flows across many projects at once. In the first week after ATR profiles became accessible via API, one customer applied them to 136 projects, saving significant time.A single profile turns on flows like false-positive detection, risk contextualization, and vulnerability resolution. Security managers choose one of three presets — Conservative, Standard, or Proactive — to set which severity levels each flow addresses and whether it runs automatically or only on demand.Until now, applying an ATR profile required writing a script. In 19.6, security managers select projects by group or attribute from the Security Inventory or the security configuration page, choose a profile, and apply it. Afterward, Security Inventory shows which projects have a flow turned on, alongside their scanner coverage.   ATR profiles are available to GitLab Ultimate customers on all GitLab offerings. To use them, follow the ATR profile setup steps.Assess the exploitability of SAST findings with Vulnerability Context FlowWithout exposure context, a SAST finding in an isolated internal service looks as urgent as the same finding in a public-facing service that handles sensitive data.Vulnerability Context Flow identifies and analyzes the affected service, even in a monorepo, and adds a risk table to the SAST finding. The table shows whether exploiting the flaw requires authentication or elevated authorization, whether the service handles sensitive data, and whether it is exposed to untrusted input. Teams can then rank the backlog by exploitability as well as severity.   Vulnerability Context Flow is in beta for GitLab Ultimate customers on all GitLab offerings in 19.6. To turn it on, follow the Vulnerability Context Flow setup.See mean time to remediation at a glanceSecurity leaders track MTTR to understand how long vulnerabilities stay open and whether that window is shrinking. The security dashboard now charts weekly MTTR for findings in first-party code and third-party dependencies, at the project, group, and organization level. items.title: Duo Agent Platform now does up to 2x more per GitLab Credit
items.summary: GitLab Duo Agent Platform has become more efficient in how it uses the underlying models offered through GitLab. That includes all the latest models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and GitLab-hosted open-weight models.And, we’re passing the savings to you.Each task you give to agents and flows in GitLab now results in fewer model requests. Enable prompt caching and eligible tasks use even fewer requests. Together, these efficiencies mean most customers will see their GitLab Credits go up to twice as far.What this looks like in real lifeAs a representative example, consider the following example of a real team of 500 people using GitLab Duo Agent Platform in October 2026. Across every use case, the number of requests they were billed for (Column 2) is higher than what it would be with the new efficiencies turned on (Column 4). Therefore, the GitLab Credits used moving forward (same request to credit ratios by model type) will be lower.Your GitLab account team can show how your recent usage compares with the new efficiencies enabled, so you can see how much further your credits will go.Put the extra credits to workWith fewer credits required for your current use cases, you can enable more agents and flows, and automate more steps in your software development lifecycle, natively integrated in the GitLab platform you already use. Here are some good places to start:Turn Slack conversations into shipped work. GitLab for Slack now has agent capabilities. Mention @GitLab in a team channel or your own DM, and the agent reads the conversation, checks what already exists in GitLab, turns decisions into issues and merge requests, and starts agent flows, posting the results back to the thread. Each request runs with your own GitLab permissions and is recorded as an agent session.Put routine work on a schedule. With scheduled automations, now in beta in GitLab 19.6, flows run on their own at a cadence your team sets, from every 15 minutes to every three months. Triage new issues every morning, or check CI health every hour and comment with the likely root cause before anyone opens the incident.Find the flaws other scanners miss. The Business Logic Security Analyzer, now in beta for GitLab Ultimate on GitLab.com, scans repositories and merge requests for authorization and access-control vulnerabilities that pattern-based scanners can miss. To power this flow with Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5.2, contact your account team.Turn issues into merge requests. Duo Developer takes an issue to a ready-to-review merge request, following the issue’s plan in your project’s context. Start it from an issue or a discussion in GitLab, have it start automatically when a work item changes status, or work with it directly from the Duo CLI. Every session is recorded in GitLab. Because these sessions are long and context-heavy, they benefit most from the new efficiencies, especially with prompt caching enabled.Hand off a whole objective with /goal. In the Duo CLI or Duo Agent Platform Chat, describe what you want done with /goal, and GitLab Duo plans the work, carries it out and checks the result, using an independent judge to decide when the goal is met. You stay in control throughout and can pause, change the goal, or redirect the agent at any point.If you’re using credits as part of a GitLab Flex agreement, you can also use those freed-up credits for recently released capabilities such as GitLab Secrets Manager, Dedicated Runners, GitLab Orbit (coming soon), and more innovations.More value, more visibility, more control over your spendThese efficiencies build on recent launches that help you see where credits go, set budget guardrails, and direct your spend as priorities change.See where your investment is going. The Duo Agent Platform Impact dashboard, introduced in GitLab 19.5, brings adoption, work activity, and credit consumption into one view. Break down consumption by model, flow type, and group or project to inform where you expand next.Set guardrails as adoption grows. The Credit caps page, introduced in GitLab 19.4 for GitLab.com and Self-Managed, lets you set a default per-user credit cap and individual overrides without using an API. This gives teams room to experiment while managing how much each user can consume.Give every user visibility into their own usage. Individual users on GitLab.com can now track their own GitLab Credits consumption over time, filtered by product and date range, without relying on an administrator’s report.Keep your budget flexible with GitLab FlexAs you discover where agents deliver the most value, your spending priorities will evolve too.GitLab Flex brings seats and GitLab Credits together under one annual commitment, with flexibility to adjust your monthly allocation within your agreement. It helps you direct your investment toward the capabilities your teams need as adoption grows.More value from each credit, combined with more flexibility in how you use your budget, gives you room to expand without

items.title: The best way to use your coding agents with GitLab
items.summary: Say you and your team already use Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Devin, or OpenCode to write code. Maybe even more than one of them.What happens next depends on everyone’s personal setup.Some have their agent review changes, watch CI pipelines and security checks, with a different approach to follow up when something breaks. Others do it by hand. When those steps depend on each engineer’s setup, skill, or time to follow up, even changes in the same project move at different speeds and get different levels of scrutiny.We paired each one of these coding agents to create a recommended configuration that makes your best engineering practices the default for the whole team.One bar for every change. You set security, architecture, and engineering standards once in GitLab. Duo reviews changes against your review instructions, and GitLab enforces required pipelines, security checks, and approvals before merge, whether a coding agent or a person wrote the change.Give agents the context they need. Duo can work from the repository, merge request discussion, CI logs, and scanner results. Your team doesn’t have to piece that context back together every time work moves between tools or people.Delegation without handing over keys. Composite identity ties every agent action to the agent and the person who started it, and limits access to what both are allowed to do.Leave a record the next engineer can use. Reviews, pipeline results, and approvals stay with the merge request. A pipeline fix can link back to its Duo session. Anyone picking up the work can see what ran and what still needs attention without reconstructing someone else’s agent conversation.Your models, your cloud. Pick the model for each agentic flow from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or open-weight providers, and change it when a better one ships.What’s newYour coding agent writes the code. GitLab Duo does the work that starts at the merge request and follows through to deployment.You can now set up code review, pipeline repair, and security triage together from your coding session. The GitLab Duo setup skill connects your agent to GitLab and configures automatic review and failed-pipeline repair. On the Ultimate tier, you can also opt in to security triage and remediation. The skill tells you what, if anything, still needs your attention.Once configured, the work keeps running in GitLab even if you close your editor. When you come back, the optional MR follow-up skill checks what’s already running and brings review and pipeline feedback back into your coding session.For a deep dive on how to use our new skills, please see our detailed guide here.What you and your team getGive every eligible MR a separate review for 25¢Your coding agent can check its own work before it pushes. Duo gives the change a second look when the MR is marked ready and posts feedback on the diff. A review costs a flat $0.25 at list price, so 1,000 reviews cost $250. Anthropic's Code Review averages $15–$25 a review, so the same volume would cost $15,000 or more. That makes a first pass practical even for routine changes.Then ask your agent to read the comments, fix the ones you agree with, and reply on each thread.Turn security findings into fixes you can verifyOn Ultimate, Duo flags likely false positives from static application security testing and secret detection and opens MRs with fixes for eligible SAST findings, usually about 10 minutes after a scan. Your team gets a proposed change it can test, scan, and review under the same rules as any other change.Start investigating when CI goes redWhen a pipeline fails, an automation starts Fix CI/CD Pipeline while you're on to something else, and links the session on the MR. Duo suggests a change, opens a fix MR, or explains what it found if it can't propose a reliable fix. The fix still has to pass CI. While Duo works on the fix on GitLab, your coding harness can also collaborate with Duo to review the proposed fix, commit a change to the MR, and watch for the pipeline to pass.Take an MR to merge, with policy-based approvalsThe MR follow-up skill checks the review threads, failed jobs, and conflicts on an MR, and works through them from your agent. Your agent can resolve a merge conflict in your checkout, or hand it to the Developer flow to resolve in GitLab. The skill stops when only approvals are left.Then your approval rules decide what merges, for agent changes and people alike. Approval policies can require a person to approve every MR, or add approvers when a scan finds a vulnerability. Pipeline execution policies make required jobs run. Tool approval guardrails can make an agent ask a person before a sensitive action. Tool calls that go through GitLab’s MCP server can be viewed in Audit events when storage is enabled. If you let Duo approve MRs, its approval doesn't count toward required approvals.Hand an issue to GitLab Duo and get back a merge requestAsk your agent to hand an assigned issue to the Developer flow. The flow runs in GitL
